title: When is the quietest time to visit Lapland?
author: Brogan
intro: Lapland is busiest in the weeks before Christmas, when charter flights, day trips and families all arrive at once. Go at the right time and you get the same snow, reindeer and northern lights with far fewer people and lower prices.
seo_title: Quietest time to visit Lapland (and still get snow)
seo_description: When Lapland is least busy, month by month: crowds, prices, daylight, cold and northern lights, plus the quiet weeks that still have reliable snow.

sections.heading: The short answer
sections.text:
The quietest times to visit Lapland **with snow** are:

- **The first three weeks of January**, once the New Year crowds go home. It's the coldest and darkest time, but prices drop sharply.
- **Early to mid March**, outside Finnish school holidays. There's deep snow, much more daylight, and it's less bitterly cold.
- **Late November**, before most Christmas charter flights start. Snow isn't guaranteed yet, especially in the south of Lapland.

The busiest are **December**, especially the middle of the month up to New Year, and the **February half-term week**. If you can only go at Christmas, pick a weekday early in December over the week before Christmas.

sections.heading: Month by month
sections.text:
- **Late August to October:** autumn colours (called *ruska* in Finland) in September, and the northern lights start as nights get dark. Very quiet, but no snow.
- **November:** quiet until the last week or so, when Christmas season starts. Snow usually arrives during the month but can be patchy, especially around [Rovaniemi](/destinations/rovaniemi).
- **December:** peak season. UK charter flights and day trips, school groups and families from all over Europe fill Rovaniemi and the resorts. Prices for hotels, cabins and activities are at their highest.
- **January:** the quietest winter month after the first week. Expect hard frosts (well below -15°C is common) and very short days.
- **February:** busy again in the UK half-term week, and some weeks get Finnish school ski-holiday crowds.
- **March:** the best all-round month for many people. Deep snow, long bright days, and quieter outside the Finnish school holidays.
- **April:** spring skiing in the northern resorts, thinning crowds, but the northern lights season ends as nights get too light.
- **May:** the snow melts and many activities pause. The quietest month of all, with good reason.
- **June to mid-August:** midnight sun and hiking, with no snow and few tourists.

sections.heading: Why December is so busy
sections.text:
Lapland's reputation in the UK is built on Christmas. In December, extra seasonal flights arrive from the UK, and tour operators run Santa trips, from day trips to four-night breaks. Santa Claus Village in Rovaniemi, which is open all year, gets its biggest crowds, and husky and reindeer rides book up weeks ahead.

If you're set on seeing Santa, January works well: he's still there, the queues are shorter, the snow is deeper, and many of the activities are the same. If December is the only option, book activities as early as you can and choose a weekday to visit Santa Claus Village.

sections.heading: Watch out for school holidays
sections.text:
Two sets of school holidays change the picture:

- **UK February half-term** sends a lot of British families to Lapland, so that week is busy and expensive.
- **Finnish winter holidays** (*hiihtoloma*) run for a week in February or March, staggered by region. Ski resorts like [Levi](/destinations/levi) and [Saariselkä](/destinations/saariselka) get particularly busy with Finnish families then.

Check the Finnish school holiday dates for the year you're travelling before booking a ski trip in late February or early March. The week after the last region's holiday is usually one of the quietest snowy weeks of the season.

sections.heading: Daylight, cold and the northern lights
sections.text:
Quiet seasons come with trade-offs:

- **Daylight:** around the shortest day, Rovaniemi gets only two or three hours of daylight. Further north, Levi and Saariselkä have a stretch around midwinter when the sun doesn't rise above the horizon at all, though there's a blue twilight in the middle of the day. By early March there are more than ten hours of daylight.
- **Cold:** January is usually the coldest month, and nights can fall well below -25°C. Most tour operators lend thermal outer layers, but you'll still need good base layers, mitts and boots.
- **Northern lights:** the season runs from roughly late August to early April. You need dark, clear skies, so long, cold nights in January are good for seeing them, and March balances good chances with milder evenings. No month guarantees them.

If the aurora is the main reason for your trip, quieter months don't hurt your chances at all, and fewer people means darker, emptier viewing spots.

sections.heading: Quieter alternatives to Rovaniemi
sections.text:
If you want Lapland without the crowds at any time of year:

- **[Saariselkä](/destinations/saariselka)**, in the far north of Finland, is smaller and quieter than Rovaniemi or Levi, with fells for skiing and good aurora odds.
- **[Kiruna](/destinations/kiruna)** in Swedish Lapland, close to Abisko and the Icehotel, feels less built around Christmas.
- **[Tromsø](/destinations/tromso)** in Arctic Norway has whale watching in winter and a lively small city, but it's more expensive.

Our comparisons of [Rovaniemi, Levi or Saariselkä](/blog/rovaniemi-levi-or-saariselka) and [Tromsø or Rovaniemi](/blog/tromso-or-rovaniemi) go into more detail.

sections.heading: How to pick your dates
sections.text:
Start with what matters most:

- **Santa and snow, on a budget:** the second or third week of January.
- **Skiing, daylight and milder cold:** early to mid March, avoiding Finnish holiday weeks.
- **Northern lights first:** January to March, away from the full moon.
- **It has to be December:** early December, midweek, with activities booked well ahead.

If your family is torn between Lapland in December and something else entirely, our [Christmas holidays](/destinations/christmas-holidays) and [January](/destinations/where-to-go-in-january) pages have more ideas. Put the options on a somewhere.party list and let everyone vote.

faqs.question: What is the cheapest time to go to Lapland?
faqs.answer: For a snowy trip, January after the first week is usually the cheapest, followed by early March outside Finnish school holidays. December is the most expensive time.

faqs.question: Is Santa in Lapland in January?
faqs.answer: Yes. Santa Claus Village in Rovaniemi is open all year, and January is much quieter than December.

faqs.question: When is the best time to see the northern lights in Lapland?
faqs.answer: The season runs from about late August to early April. January to March is often best, because the nights are long and snow makes it easier to get around, but clear skies matter most.

faqs.question: Is there snow in Lapland in November?
faqs.answer: Usually by late November, but it isn't guaranteed, particularly in southern Lapland around Rovaniemi. From December to March snow is far more reliable.

faqs.question: How cold is Lapland in January?
faqs.answer: Daytime temperatures around -10°C to -20°C are common, and nights can drop below -25°C, so you need proper thermal clothing.
